title: Interception of non-viral precancers before they invade

concept.text: The innovation is a safe way to identify high-risk, non-viral precancerous cells and eliminate them, or durably stop their progression, before invasive cancer develops. Its central target is an existing premalignant clone or field of altered tissue for which local removal is unsuitable. This would extend precursor-directed prevention to settings where removing a discrete lesion cannot adequately address the biological problem.

Interception requires two linked capabilities: determining which precursors warrant intervention and treating them without causing disproportionate harm to people who do not yet have invasive cancer. The treatment could involve drugs, vaccines, immune modulation or another precursor-directed approach; the concept is defined by preventing progression, rather than by a particular treatment platform. Mapping a precursor's molecular features can enable this work, but an atlas alone does not demonstrate that progression can be prevented.

Scope clarification: this record concerns intervention after a non-viral precursor exists and before invasion. Prevention before an identifiable precursor exists is a separate capability, as is treatment of an already invasive cancer. It also does not assume that every internal precursor is inaccessible: suitability for local removal must be assessed for the particular lesion and clinical setting.

significance.text: If interception safely prevented progression in people carrying genuinely high-risk precursors, it would directly reduce invasive cancers arising from those precursors. The revolutionary advance would be to make a biologically early stage therapeutically actionable in settings that cannot be adequately managed by local removal. The supplied 2025 review describes premalignant lesions as an opportunity for intervention before malignant transformation, while emphasizing that clinical translation remains limited.

Conditional impact assessment: fewer invasive cancers could subsequently mean fewer intensive cancer treatments and fewer cancer deaths, but these outcomes would depend on which precursors are intercepted, how often they would otherwise progress, treatment harms and the duration of protection. Controlling a lesion that would have remained indolent offers little cancer-prevention benefit and can expose a person to unnecessary treatment. A large effect on overall cancer mortality therefore requires both effective therapy and accurate selection of consequential precursor states.

Existing precursor treatment provides a useful but limited analogy. The reviewed material describes effective treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, while also noting elevated subsequent cervical cancer risk. This virus-associated example illustrates the value of intervening before invasion, but neither demonstrates the proposed non-viral capability nor implies that treating one precursor abolishes a person's future cancer risk. The review also describes surgical management in selected lung and pancreatic precursor settings, so an internal anatomical location alone does not establish a need for systemic interception.

Generalization limit: success in two precursor states would establish meaningful breadth, not a general solution for all major lethal cancers. Different organs, precursor lineages and routes to progression could require different risk models and interventions. Prevention before a detectable precursor appears and treatment after invasion would remain necessary even if this capability succeeded.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is the combination of reliable progression-risk assessment and safe, durable precursor control when local removal is unsuitable. The biological problem is distinguishing lesions likely to become consequential cancers from those that remain indolent, and then identifying a vulnerability whose alteration actually prevents malignant transformation. Molecular abnormalities or a recognizable precursor state do not by themselves establish that treatment will improve outcomes.

Sampling and characterization are concrete obstacles. The reviewed material describes small premalignant foci, limited tissue obtainable through biopsy and rare tumor-initiating cells. These features make it difficult to characterize the cells responsible for progression and to validate candidate risk biomarkers and preventive targets. Multi-omic mapping helps expose precursor biology, but prospective clinical validation is still needed to connect those measurements to useful decisions and effective interventions.

Engineering requirements, proposed here, include reaching the relevant precursor population, achieving sufficient control to prevent progression, preserving normal tissue function and monitoring for persistence or recurrence. A dispersed field could present a different delivery problem from a discrete lesion, but the supplied evidence does not establish that dangerous precursors are generally dispersed. Likewise, safety must be demonstrated for the proposed preventive regimen; the available review does not establish how frequently drugs developed for invasive cancer would be unacceptably toxic in these populations.

Clinical evaluation creates a further barrier: molecular changes can be measured before an invasive-cancer outcome is available, but their meaning must be established. The 2025 review proposes surrogate indicators and intermediate molecular endpoints to make preventive studies more practical. Such endpoints can support development, yet a favorable biomarker change alone does not establish that an intervention prevents invasive cancer.

current_state.text: The principal available evidence is the October 17, 2025 review by Feiran Zhang and colleagues, Multi-Omics Meets Premalignancy: Paving the Way for Early Prevention of Cancer, DOI 10.34133/research.0930. As summarized in the supplied evidence review, it describes PreCancer Atlas and Human Tumor Atlas Network efforts to map premalignant evolution, alongside candidate chemopreventive and immune interventions. These are enabling research achievements and intervention leads; atlas construction does not itself establish successful interception.

The review reports evaluations in selected human precursor settings and preclinical intervention results. One specific example is reduced tumor burden after TIM-3 blockade at the precancerous stage in mice. That result supports biological feasibility in an experimental model, but it does not establish durable precursor eradication, prevention of invasive cancer in humans or an approved preventive treatment. The supplied evidence review provides no numerical effect size for this example, so none can be assigned here.

Established precursor management forms part of the background. The available review describes high efficacy of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia treatment with residual subsequent cancer risk, as well as surgical management of selected internal precursor settings. These observations narrow the target to situations where local removal is unsuitable or insufficient. They do not establish a broadly applicable therapy for non-viral precursors.

The 2025 review explicitly describes limited clinical implementation of insights from premalignant-lesion multi-omics and calls for prospective validation. This supports an active research program with a substantial translational gap. It does not establish either the existence or the comprehensive absence of effective non-viral interception across all settings as of November 1, 2026. No updated evidence search is included in the supplied materials.

Two additional citations require restricted interpretation. The research notes attribute an interception framework and a broad cancer-prevention-vaccine approval statement to a 2024 Domchek–Vonderheide article, and describe a purported March 13, 2026 Trends in Molecular Medicine review as discussing emerging vaccine and immune-modulator trials at abstract level. Neither source text was available to the supplied reviewer. Their wording, scope and the associated approval claim therefore remain unverified here; the citations cannot establish a current regulatory inventory or a completed interceptive therapy.

The available assessment of the 2025 review also has boundaries: its saved text extraction included the main discussion but was truncated during the references, and figures were not inspected. Its intervention examples are review-level reports rather than an independent assessment here of every underlying experiment or clinical study. These limitations restrict the detail and confidence of conclusions; they do not show that the reported results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: randomized clinical evidence in at least two non-viral precursor states for which local removal is unsuitable, selected for their contribution to cancer mortality, should show precursor elimination or durable arrest together with fewer invasive cancers and an acceptable safety profile. The choice of two states and the mortality-based selection rule are proposed benchmarks for this record, not established clinical standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and safety requirements: studies should prespecify follow-up long enough to assess progression, recurrence and delayed harms in each precursor state. They should measure normal tissue function, treatment burden and the balance between cancers prevented and people unnecessarily treated. Finite follow-up can demonstrate durable control over a defined interval; it cannot prove permanent arrest.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed durability and safety requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidentiary boundary: biomarker clearance alone would be incomplete under this record's completion criterion. Intermediate endpoints could guide early development, but convincing completion would connect precursor control to fewer invasive cancers. This is deliberately stricter than the 2025 review's practical recommendation to prioritize surrogate and intermediate molecular endpoints when evaluating preventive approaches.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed evidentiary boundary

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: independent studies or multicenter replication should confirm the benefit using reproducible precursor definitions, risk measurements and treatment procedures. Results should specify the populations, tissue states and delivery conditions in which benefit holds. Successful demonstrations would establish interception within those tested boundaries, rather than literal universality across precancers.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility requirements

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: ONC-01, Mortality-reducing detection of lethal cancers while they are still localized, concerns finding cancers early enough to improve survival. ONC-08 acts earlier, on precursors before invasion. ONC-10, A reliable distinction between early neoplasms that will kill and those that will not, overlaps directly with the risk-stratification problem: it could improve selection for interception, but prediction alone does not neutralize a precursor.

Roster-based distinction: ONC-09, Prophylactic immunity that prevents the common non-viral cancers, targets protection before an identifiable precursor exists. ONC-08 targets an existing precursor and could use immune or nonimmune methods. A vaccine directed at an established premalignant clone could contribute to interception without demonstrating the broader prophylactic capability.

Roster-based distinction: ONC-02, Sterilizing immune clearance of established metastatic carcinomas, and ONC-03, Eradication of dormant disseminated tumor cells that cause late relapse, address disease after invasion and dissemination. They may share immune-targeting or persistence problems with ONC-08, but metastatic cells and dormant disseminated tumor cells occupy a different disease stage from a noninvasive precursor.

Roster-based distinction: ONC-04, A shared malignant dependency that renewing normal tissues can spare, could contribute a selective target if a relevant vulnerability is already present in precursors. ONC-05, Therapies that drive the whole clonal population to extinction, overlaps with the eradication route to interception. ONC-08 also permits durable arrest that prevents progression, so complete clonal extinction is one possible mechanism rather than its only endpoint.

Roster-based distinction: ONC-06, Stable reversion of carcinoma cells to non-malignant tissue identity, seeks a change in the state of established carcinoma cells. A related stabilization or reversion mechanism might eventually help control precursors, but that would require separate evidence. ONC-07, Body-wide delivery that alters essentially every malignant cell, could supply useful delivery technology for dispersed precursor fields, although ONC-08's delivery requirements depend on the precursor setting and the control mechanism.

Roster-based distinction: ONC-11, Real-time, cell-resolution guidance that makes incomplete cancer surgery uncommon, improves surgical removal; ONC-08 focuses on precursors for which local removal is unsuitable. ONC-12, Off-the-shelf cell therapy that matches autologous cures and can be given at ordinary scale, could provide an intervention platform, but scalable cell therapy would still need separate evidence of preventive efficacy and acceptable safety in people with precursors.

change_log.change: Preserved ONC-08 and its title while defining the target as high-risk non-viral precursors for which local removal is unsuitable.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent, but internal anatomy alone does not establish that removal is infeasible; the reviewed material describes surgical management in selected lung and pancreatic settings.

change_log.change: Replaced permanent arrest with durable arrest over a prespecified observation period.
Integrated risk stratification, small premalignant foci, limited biopsy material and rare tumor-initiating cells into the explanation of the missing capability.
change_log.reason: These are concrete barriers supported by the supplied review and explain why mapping precursors does not immediately yield effective prevention.

change_log.change: Qualified generalized clone dispersal and toxicity assertions, and left clonal hematopoiesis as an unresolved proposed example.
change_log.reason: The supplied inspectable evidence does not establish those broader claims or the hematopoietic application.

change_log.change: Added reported human evaluations and the mouse TIM-3 blockade example while distinguishing them from durable human cancer prevention.
change_log.reason: The original atlas-focused account understated intervention research, but the available evidence does not demonstrate the full proposed capability.

change_log.change: Removed the unverified vaccine-approval quotation and treated the 2024 and 2026 citations as unavailable for substantive verification.
change_log.reason: Neither source text was supplied to the reviewer, and the purported 2026 discussion was described only at abstract level.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical present-day absence claims with a dated account of limited translation and an explicit freshness limitation.
change_log.reason: The 2025 review and empty freshness record cannot establish a comprehensive status as of November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Bounded the precursor-removal analogy by preserving residual cancer risk after cervical precursor treatment.
change_log.reason: Successful treatment of a particular lesion does not establish elimination of future cancer risk or demonstrate non-viral interception.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria to include safety, follow-up, reproducibility and practical scope, while retaining invasive-cancer reduction as the proposed endpoint.
change_log.reason: These additions make the proposal assessable without presenting its thresholds as standards or implying universality from finite trials.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry without merging concepts.
change_log.reason: Shared mechanisms, enabling technologies and neighboring disease stages do not make the concepts interchangeable.

unresolved_issues: The 2024 Domchek–Vonderheide attribution, its precise interception definition and the broad vaccine-approval statement remain unverified because the source text was not supplied.
The identity, contents and trial coverage of the purported March 13, 2026 review remain unverified; the notes describe abstract-level access but provide no captured text.
The supplied materials do not establish a comprehensive clinical or regulatory status as of November 1, 2026.
Clonal hematopoiesis remains a proposed application whose precursor definitions, progression risks and intervention evidence are not established by the available material.

Claims that most mutant clones never progress, that dangerous clones are generally dispersed and that invasive-cancer drugs are often too toxic for prevention require additional evidence or setting-specific qualification.

The human intervention evaluations summarized by the 2025 review are not described sufficiently in the supplied evidence review to determine their effect sizes, durability or invasive-cancer outcomes.
The saved 2025 extraction is truncated during the references, figures were not inspected, and underlying intervention studies were not independently assessed here.
Selection of the two precursor states, acceptable safety boundaries and adequate follow-up intervals remains to be specified; these are proposed evaluation choices rather than established standards.
